cor-a-similar-to-transpose.title_html: A Matrix Is Similar to Its Transpose
cor-a-similar-to-transpose.html: Let F be any field and A∈Mn(F). Then A∼AT.

cor-companion-linear-power-is-jordan.title: Companion Blocks of Linear Powers Are Jordan Blocks
cor-companion-linear-power-is-jordan.title_html: Companion Blocks of Linear Powers Are Jordan Blocks
cor-companion-linear-power-is-jordan.html: Let λ∈F and k≥1. Then C((x−λ)k)∼Jk(λ). Consequently, if pT splits over F, then the elementary divisors of T are the polynomials (x−λ)k for the Jordan blocks Jk(λ) of T, and the elementary divisor form of @thm-elementary-divisor-form and the Jordan form of T are obtained from one another by replacing each block C((x−λ)k) by Jk(λ) and conversely.

cor-exponential-of-jordan-block.title: Exponential of a Jordan Block, with a Parameter
cor-exponential-of-jordan-block.title_html: Exponential of a Jordan Block, with a Parameter
cor-exponential-of-jordan-block.html: Let k≥1, λ∈C and t∈R. Then etJk(λ) is the upper triangular matrix with (etJk(λ))r,r+j=tjeλtj!(0≤j≤k−1) and zeros below the diagonal. Consequently, if A=PJP−1 with J=Jk1(λ1)⊕⋯⊕Jkm(λm), then etA=P(etJk1(λ1)⊕⋯⊕etJkm(λm))P−1. In particular, for a diagonal D=diag(d1,…,dn), etD=diag(etd1,…,etdn).

cor-generalized-eigenspace-is-kernel.title: The Generalized Eigenspace Is One Kernel
cor-generalized-eigenspace-is-kernel.title_html: The Generalized Eigenspace Is One Kernel
cor-generalized-eigenspace-is-kernel.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n, let T∈L(V) and λ∈F, and put N=T−λidV with stabilization index s. Then:

  1. Gλ(T)=kerNs=kerNn;
  2. Gλ(T) is T-invariant, and Eλ(T)⊆Gλ(T);
  3. Gλ(T)≠{0} if and only if λ is an eigenvalue of T;
  4. if v∈Gλ(T) is non-zero and k≥1 is least with Nkv=0, then Nk−1v is an eigenvector of T for λ.

cor-invariant-factors-are-smith-entries.title: The Smith Form of xI - A Carries the Invariant Factors
cor-invariant-factors-are-smith-entries.title_html: The Smith Form of xI−A Carries the Invariant Factors
cor-invariant-factors-are-smith-entries.html: Let A∈Mn(F) with invariant factors d1∣d2∣⋯∣dr as in @thm-rational-canonical-form. Then the Smith normal form of xI−A is diag(1,…,1⏟n−r,d1,d2,…,dr). In particular the invariant factors of A are exactly the non-constant diagonal entries of the Smith normal form of xI−A, read from the top down, and two matrices in Mn(F) are similar if and only if xI−A and xI−B have the same Smith normal form.

cor-invariant-factors-unique.title: Uniqueness of the Chain and of the Prime Powers
cor-invariant-factors-unique.title_html: Uniqueness of the Chain and of the Prime Powers
cor-invariant-factors-unique.html:
Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F and T∈L(V).

  1. Any two decompositions as in @thm-cyclic-decomposition give the same ordered list d1∣⋯∣dr.
  2. Any decomposition V=Z(u1;T)⊕⋯⊕Z(uN;T) whose annihilators mT,ui are powers of monic irreducibles gives the same list of annihilators, up to order, namely the prime powers occurring in d1,…,dr.
  3. Explicitly, writing cp(k)=dim⁡kerp(T)k−dim⁡kerp(T)k−1deg⁡p(p monic irreducible, k≥1), the list is recovered by r=maxpcp(1) and vp(dj)=#{k≥1:cp(k)≥r+1−j}(1≤j≤r). In particular the invariant factors of T are determined by the numbers dim⁡kerp(T)k alone.

cor-jordan-invariants.title: Invariants from the Jordan Form
cor-jordan-invariants.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, let T∈L(V) with pT split, let J be a Jordan form of T, and let λ∈F. Then:

  1. aT(λ) is the sum of the sizes of the λ-blocks of J; in particular λ∈spec(T) if and only if J has a λ-block;
  2. gT(λ) is the number of λ-blocks of J;
  3. the exponent of x−λ in mT is the largest size of a λ-block of J (and 0 when J has no λ-block);
  4. dim⁡ker(T−λidV)j=∑min(ki,j), summed over the sizes ki of the λ-blocks, for every j≥0;
  5. T is diagonalizable if and only if every block of J has size 1, that is, if and only if J is diagonal.

cor-markov-powers-converge.title: Convergence of a Markov Chain
cor-markov-powers-converge.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic (@def-stochastic-matrix), n≥1. Then:

  1. (Am) is bounded; consequently every eigenvalue λ∈C of A satisfies |λ|≤1, and every eigenvalue with |λ|=1 has only 1×1 blocks. In particular aA(1)=gA(1).
  2. (Am) converges if and only if 1 is the only eigenvalue of A of modulus 1; and then limmAm is the projection onto E1(A) along ⨁λ≠1Gλ(A).

cor-nilpotent-similar-iff-ranks.title: Similarity of Nilpotent Matrices
cor-nilpotent-similar-iff-ranks.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F), n≥1, both nilpotent. Then A∼B if and only if rankAj=rankBjfor every j=1,2,…,n−1. Equivalently, A∼B if and only if their chain lengths, as lists in decreasing order, agree.

cor-real-block-complex-jordan.title: A Real Jordan Block Splits into Two Complex Ones
cor-real-block-complex-jordan.title_html: A Real Jordan Block Splits into Two Complex Ones
cor-real-block-complex-jordan.html: Let λ∉R and k≥1. Then, as matrices over C, Ck(λ)∼Jk(λ)⊕Jk(λ―). In particular pCk(λ)=((x−λ)(x−λ―))k, the polynomial ((x−a)2+b2)k∈R[x], and mCk(λ) is the same polynomial.

cor-similar-iff-same-invariant-factors.title: Similarity via the Invariant Factors
cor-similar-iff-same-invariant-factors.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with n≥1. The following are equivalent:

  1. A∼B;
  2. A and B have the same invariant factors;
  3. A and B have the same elementary divisors, up to order;
  4. dim⁡kerp(A)k=dim⁡kerp(B)k for every monic irreducible p∈F[x] and every k≥1.

cor-similar-iff-same-jordan-form.title: Similarity via the Jordan Form
cor-similar-iff-same-jordan-form.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F), n≥1, and suppose pA splits over F. The following are equivalent:

  1. A∼B;
  2. pB splits over F, and A and B have the same Jordan form, up to the order of the blocks;
  3. pA=pB and rank(A−λI)j=rank(B−λI)j for every λ∈spec(A) and every j=1,…,n.

cor-similarity-field-independent.title: Similarity Is Independent of the Field
cor-similarity-field-independent.title_html: Similarity Is Independent of the Field
cor-similarity-field-independent.html: Let K be a subfield of L and let A,B∈Mn(K), n≥1. If A and B are similar over L, then they are similar over K: A=Q−1BQ  for some invertible Q∈Mn(L)⟹A=P−1BP  for some invertible P∈Mn(K).

def-companion-matrix.title: Companion Matrix
def-companion-matrix.html: Let n≥1 and let p=xn+an−1xn−1+⋯+a1x+a0∈F[x] be monic of degree n. The companion matrix of p is the matrix C(p)∈Mn(F) with 1 in each position (j+1,j) just below the diagonal, last column (−a0,−a1,…,−an−1), and 0 elsewhere: C(p)=(00⋯0−a010⋯0−a101⋯0−a2⋮⋱⋮00⋯1−an−1). For n=1 and p=x+a0 this reads C(p)=(−a0).

def-cyclic-subspace.title: Cyclic Subspace
def-cyclic-subspace.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let T∈L(V) and let v∈V. The cyclic subspace generated by v is Z(v;T):=span(v, Tv, T2v, …)=span({Tjv:j≥0}), where T0=idV. For A∈Mn(F) we write Z(v;A)=Z(v;TA).

def-cyclic-vector.title: Cyclic Vector, Cyclic Operator
def-cyclic-vector.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V). A vector v∈V is a cyclic vector for T if Z(v;T)=V. We call T cyclic if it has a cyclic vector, and A∈Mn(F) cyclic if TA is.

def-entrywise-convergence.title: Entrywise Convergence and Boundedness
def-entrywise-convergence.html:
Let M1,M2,… be matrices in Mp×q(C) and M∈Mp×q(C).

  1. The sequence (Mm) converges to M, written Mm→M, if for every position (r,s) the sequence of complex numbers (Mm)rs converges to Mrs. We then write M=limmMm.
  2. The sequence (Mm) is bounded if there is a real c≥0 with |(Mm)rs|≤c for all m and all positions (r,s).
  3. A series ∑k≥0Mk converges to M if its sequence of partial sums ∑k=0KMk converges to M.

def-generalized-eigenspace.title: Generalized Eigenspace
def-generalized-eigenspace.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let T∈L(V) and λ∈F. The generalized eigenspace of T for λ is Gλ(T):={v∈V:(T−λidV)kv=0 for some integer k≥1}=⋃k≥1ker(T−λidV)k. For A∈Mn(F) we write Gλ(A)=Gλ(TA).

def-generalized-eigenvector.title: Generalized Eigenvector
def-generalized-eigenvector.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let T∈L(V) and λ∈F. A generalized eigenvector of T for λ is a vector v∈V with v≠0 such that (T−λidV)kv=0for some integer k≥1.

def-invariant-factors.title: Invariant Factors, Elementary Divisors
def-invariant-factors.html: Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F and T∈L(V). The invariant factors of T are the monic non-constant polynomials d1∣d2∣⋯∣dr of @thm-cyclic-decomposition, which by @cor-invariant-factors-unique (a) do not depend on the decomposition. The elementary divisors of T are the prime powers occurring in the factorizations of d1,…,dr, listed with repetition; by @cor-invariant-factors-unique (b) they are the annihilators of the pieces in any decomposition of V into cyclic subspaces with prime-power annihilators. For A∈Mn(F) the invariant factors and elementary divisors are those of TA.

def-jordan-block.title: Jordan Block
def-jordan-block.html: Let k≥1 and λ∈F. The Jordan block of size k for λ is the matrix Jk(λ):=λIk+Jk(0)=(λ1λ⋱⋱1λ)∈Mk(F), with λ in every diagonal entry, 1 in every superdiagonal entry (j,j+1), and 0 elsewhere. In particular J1(λ)=(λ).

def-jordan-chain.title: Jordan Chain
def-jordan-chain.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let N∈L(V) and let u∈V with u≠0. Suppose Nku=0 and Nk−1u≠0 for an integer k≥1. The Jordan chain generated by u is the ordered list (Nk−1u, Nk−2u, …, Nu, u), of length k, and u is called the top of the chain. For T∈L(V) and λ∈F, a Jordan chain of T for λ means a Jordan chain of N=T−λidV.

def-jordan-form.title: Jordan Matrix, Jordan Basis, Jordan Form
def-jordan-form.title_html: Jordan Matrix, Jordan Basis, Jordan Form
def-jordan-form.html: A Jordan matrix is a matrix of the form J=Jk1(λ1)⊕Jk2(λ2)⊕⋯⊕Jkm(λm) for some m≥1, sizes ki≥1 and scalars λi∈F, not assumed distinct. Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1 and T∈L(V). A Jordan form of T is a Jordan matrix J with [T]B=J for some basis B of V; such a basis is called a Jordan basis for T. For A∈Mn(F), a Jordan form of A is a Jordan matrix J with A∼J.

def-matrix-exponential.title: Matrix Exponential
def-matrix-exponential.html: Let A∈Mn(C). The matrix exponential of A is eA:=∑m=0∞Amm!=limM→∞ ∑m=0MAmm!, the limit taken entrywise, provided it exists; A0=I.

def-matrix-function-jordan.title: Function of a Matrix
def-matrix-function-jordan.html: Let A∈Mn(C) with Jordan form J=Jk1(λ1)⊕⋯⊕Jkm(λm) and A=PJP−1. Let f be a complex-valued function that is defined and at least ki−1 times differentiable at λi for every i — for instance, a function given by a convergent power series on a disc around each eigenvalue. Define f(Jk(λ)):=(f(λ)f′(λ)f″(λ)2!⋯f(k−1)(λ)(k−1)!f(λ)f′(λ)⋱⋮⋱⋱f″(λ)2!f(λ)f′(λ)f(λ))∈Mk(C), the upper triangular matrix with f(j)(λ)/j! in every position (r,r+j), and f(A):=P(f(Jk1(λ1))⊕⋯⊕f(Jkm(λm)))P−1.

def-nilpotent.title: Nilpotent Operator, Index of Nilpotency
def-nilpotent.html: Let V be a vector space over F and N∈L(V). We say N is nilpotent if Ns=0for some integer s≥1. If V≠{0} and N is nilpotent, the index of nilpotency of N is the least such s; equivalently, Ns=0 and Ns−1≠0. A matrix A∈Mn(F) is nilpotent if As=0 for some s≥1, that is, if TA is nilpotent.

def-partition-of-n.title: Partition of an Integer, Young Diagram, Dual Partition
def-partition-of-n.title_html: Partition of an Integer, Young Diagram, Dual Partition
def-partition-of-n.html: Let n≥1. A partition of n is a finite list of integers k1≥k2≥⋯≥kr≥1withk1+k2+⋯+kr=n. Its Young diagram is the left-justified array of n boxes with ki boxes in row i. The dual partition k1∗≥k2∗≥… is the list of column lengths of the diagram, kj∗=#{i:ki≥j}, which is again a partition of n.

def-polynomial-elementary-operations.title: Elementary Operations over F\lbrack x\rbrack
def-polynomial-elementary-operations.title_html: Elementary Operations over F[x]
def-polynomial-elementary-operations.html:
Let M∈Mn(F[x]). An elementary row operation over F[x] on M is one of:

  1. interchanging two rows;
  2. multiplying one row by a non-zero scalar c∈F;
  3. adding h times one row to a different row, where h∈F[x] is any polynomial.

Elementary column operations over F[x] are defined the same way with “column” in place of “row”.

def-polynomial-matrix-equivalence.title: Equivalence over F\lbrack x\rbrack
def-polynomial-matrix-equivalence.title_html: Equivalence over F[x]
def-polynomial-matrix-equivalence.html: Let M,M′∈Mn(F[x]). We say M and M′ are equivalent over F[x], written M≈M′, if there are U,V∈Mn(F[x]), each invertible in Mn(F[x]), with M′=UMV.

def-real-jordan-block.title: Rotation-Scaling Block, Real Jordan Block
def-real-jordan-block.html: Let λ=a+bi∈C with a,b∈R and b≠0. The rotation-scaling block of the conjugate pair {λ,λ―} is Λ(λ):=(a−bba)∈M2(R). For an integer k≥1, the real Jordan block of size k for the pair {λ,λ―} is the matrix Ck(λ)∈M2k(R), partitioned into k×k blocks of size 2×2, with Λ(λ) in every diagonal block, I2 in every superdiagonal block, and the zero matrix elsewhere: Ck(λ):=(Λ(λ)I2Λ(λ)⋱⋱I2Λ(λ)). A real Jordan matrix is a direct sum of ordinary Jordan blocks Jk(μ) with μ∈R and real Jordan blocks Ck(λ) with λ∉R and Imλ>0.

def-semisimple-operator.title: Semisimple Operator
def-semisimple-operator.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, and let T∈L(V). We say T is semisimple if mT=p1p2⋯pk for distinct monic irreducible p1,…,pk∈F[x]; equivalently, if no irreducible polynomial p∈F[x] satisfies p2∣mT. A matrix A∈Mn(F) is semisimple over F if TA is.

def-t-annihilator.title: The T-Annihilator of a Vector
def-t-annihilator.title_html: The T-Annihilator of a Vector
def-t-annihilator.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V) and let v∈V. The set Iv:={p∈F[x]:p(T)v=0} is a non-zero ideal of F[x], and the T-annihilator of v, written mT,v, is its unique monic generator: Iv=⟨mT,v⟩. Equivalently, mT,v is the monic polynomial of least degree with mT,v(T)v=0. For A∈Mn(F) we write mA,v.

def-weyr-form.title: Basic Weyr Matrix, Weyr Structure, Weyr Form
def-weyr-form.title_html: Basic Weyr Matrix, Weyr Structure, Weyr Form
def-weyr-form.html: Let λ∈F and let w1≥w2≥⋯≥ws≥1 be a partition of an integer m≥1 (@def-partition-of-n). The basic Weyr matrix with eigenvalue λ and Weyr structure (w1,…,ws) is the matrix W∈Mm(F), partitioned into blocks according to m=w1+⋯+ws, whose blocks are Wjj=λIwj,Wj,j+1=(Iwj+10)∈Mwj×wj+1(F),Wjl=0  otherwise. A Weyr matrix is a direct sum of basic Weyr matrices. A Weyr form of T∈L(V) is a Weyr matrix W with [T]B=W for some basis B of V; for A∈Mn(F), a Weyr form of A is a Weyr matrix similar to A.

exr-convergent-matrices-c2.title: C2: Chapter 8’s Markov theorem without diagonalizability
exr-convergent-matrices-c2.title_html: C2: Chapter 8’s Markov theorem without diagonalizability
exr-convergent-matrices-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic with aA(1)=1 and |λ|<1 for every eigenvalue λ≠1.

  1. Prove that 1Tw=0 for every w∈Gλ(A) with λ≠1. Hint: 1T(A−λI)=(1−λ)1T.
  2. Prove that (Am) converges to a stochastic matrix Π, and deduce that A has a steady state v with E1(A)=span(v).
  3. Deduce that Π=v1T and that Amx0→v for every probability vector x0, without assuming that A is diagonalizable.

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: A1
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
1. Define Z(v;T) and the T-annihilator mT,v.
  2. State the formula for dim⁡Z(v;T) and say which basis of Z(v;T) the theorem provides.
  3. Write down C(p) for p=x3−2x+5, and say what pC(p) and mC(p) are.
  4. True or false: every operator on a space of dimension n≥2 has a cyclic vector. Justify your answer.
  5. What is mT,v when v is an eigenvector of T for λ? What is Z(v;T) then?
  6. True or false: if mT,v=mT for some v, then v is a cyclic vector. Justify your answer.

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: B1: Annihilators of vectors
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
Let A=(111011002)∈M3(Q).

  1. Write down pA.
  2. Find mA,e1, mA,e2 and mA,e3.
  3. For each of the three vectors, give dim⁡Z(ej;A) and identify the subspace.
  4. Write down the matrix of TA restricted to Z(e2;A) in the basis (e2,Ae2), and say which companion matrix it is.

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: B2: Cyclic or not?
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
Determine whether each matrix is cyclic. For those that are, find a cyclic vector; for those that are not, say which condition fails.

  1. diag(1,2,3)∈M3(Q).
  2. diag(1,1,2)∈M3(Q).
  3. B=(210020111)∈M3(Q), for which pB=mB=(x−2)2(x−1). Check first that none of e1,e2,e3 is cyclic.
  4. J2(0)⊕J1(0)∈M3(Q).

Hint: for (c), compute the three annihilators mB,ej and use @lem-annihilator-of-sum.

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: B3: Cyclic subspaces for differentiation
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
Let V=R[x]≤3 and let D∈L(V) be differentiation.

  1. Find mD,q for q=1, q=x, q=x2 and q=x3.
  2. Find Z(x2;D) and the matrix of D restricted to it in the basis (x2,Dx2,D2x2).
  3. Is x3 a cyclic vector for D? What is mD?

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: C1: What commutes with a cyclic operator
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title_html: C1: What commutes with a cyclic operator
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1 and let T∈L(V) satisfy mT=pT.

  1. Prove that every S∈L(V) with ST=TS is a polynomial in T, that is, S=q(T) for some q∈F[x].
  2. Deduce that the set {S∈L(V):ST=TS} is a subspace of L(V) of dimension exactly n.
  3. Show that (a) fails without the hypothesis mT=pT, by taking T=idV with n≥2.

Hint for (a): apply S to a cyclic vector.

exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.title: C2: How many cyclic vectors?
exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matri.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1 and T∈L(V).

  1. Prove that v is a cyclic vector for T if and only if v lies in no T-invariant subspace U with U≠V.
  2. Prove that if v is cyclic, then so is cv for every c∈F with c≠0. Deduce that over an infinite field a cyclic operator has infinitely many cyclic vectors.
  3. Let F=F2 and T=TJ with J=(1101). Find all cyclic vectors of T.
  4. Deduce from (c) that the set of cyclic vectors, together with 0, need not be a subspace.

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-a1.title: A1
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-a1.html:
1. State the formula for p(Jk(λ)) and say where the factorials come from.
  2. Define f(A) for A∈Mn(C) with a given Jordan form, and list the two choices whose irrelevance has to be checked.
  3. Which values of f and its derivatives does f(A) depend on? How many numbers is that?
  4. State the five properties of eA proved in @thm-exponential-properties, with their hypotheses.
  5. True or false: eA+B=eAeB for all A,B∈Mn(C). Justify your answer.
  6. True or false: eA can be singular. Justify your answer.

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b1.title: B1: Computing exponentials
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b1.html:
Compute etA for each of the following.

  1. A=(1331).
  2. A=(5105).
  3. A=(310031003)=J3(3).

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b2.title: B2: Solving systems
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b2.html:
Solve each initial value problem, and verify your answer by differentiating.

  1. x′=x+3y, y′=3x+y, with x(0)=2, y(0)=0.
  2. x′=(0−330)x with x(0)=(0,1).
  3. y‴=0 with y(0)=1, y′(0)=0, y″(0)=2, by turning it into a system.

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b3.title: B3: A square root and a logarithm
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b3.title_html: B3: A square root and a logarithm
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-b3.html:
1. Let A=(2112). Compute f(A) for f(x)=x (positive branch) and verify that f(A)2=A.
  2. Let B=(1201). Compute f(B) for f(x)=log⁡x with log⁡1=0, and verify that ef(B)=B.
  3. Explain why the same method produces no square root of (0100).

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c1.title: C1: How badly the exponential law fails
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c1.title_html: C1: How badly the exponential law fails
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c1.html:
Let A=(0100) and B=(0010) in M2(R).

  1. Compute eA, eB, eAeB and eBeA.
  2. Compute eA+B in closed form. Hint: (A+B)2=I, so split the series into even and odd terms.
  3. Verify deteA+B=etr(A+B) and det(eAeB)=etrAetrB, and explain why equal determinants do not rescue the identity.
  4. Show that eAeB=eC for some C∈M2(R), and find trC.

exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c2.title: C2: When does every solution die out?
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c2.title_html: C2: When does every solution die out?
exr-functions-of-matrices-and-odes-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C). Prove that the following are equivalent:

  1. every solution of x′=Ax satisfies x(t)→0 entrywise as t→∞;
  2. every eigenvalue λ of A has Reλ<0.

Hint: compute the entries of etJk(λ) and use (A5). For the failing direction, an eigenvector gives a solution you can write down.

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-a1.title: A1
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-a1.html:
1. Define a generalized eigenvector and the generalized eigenspace Gλ(T).
  2. State what @thm-kernel-chain-stabilizes says about the chain kerN⊆kerN2⊆…, including the bound on where it stabilizes.
  3. True or false: every generalized eigenvector of T for λ satisfies Tv=λv. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if λ is not an eigenvalue of T, then Gλ(T)={0}. Justify your answer.
  5. Let dim⁡V=6 and let pT=(x−1)4(x−3)2 split over F. What are dim⁡G1(T) and dim⁡G3(T)?
  6. In the situation of (e), what can you say about dim⁡E1(T)?

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b1.title: B1: Computing generalized eigenspaces
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b1.html:
For each operator, find all generalized eigenspaces, and compare each with the corresponding eigenspace.

  1. A1=(3103)∈M2(Q).
  2. A2=(21101−1−1−11)∈M3(R), which has mA2=(x−1)2(x−2) (@exr-primary-decomposition-b2).
  3. D∈L(R[x]≤3), differentiation.
  4. The rotation R=(0−110), first over R and then over C.

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b2.title: B2: The image chain stabilizes too
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b2.title_html: B2: The image chain stabilizes too
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n, and let N∈L(V).

  1. Prove that imN⊇imN2⊇imN3⊇…, and that each imNk is N-invariant.
  2. Prove that imNm=imNm+1 if and only if kerNm=kerNm+1.
  3. Deduce that imNn=imNn+j for every j≥0, and that the image chain stabilizes at exactly the same index s as the kernel chain.

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b3.title: B3: Reading the dimensions off a triangular matrix
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b3.title_html: B3: Reading the dimensions off a triangular matrix
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-b3.html:
Let A=(1100011000210002)∈M4(Q).

  1. Write down pA and the algebraic multiplicities.
  2. Compute E1(A), G1(A), E2(A) and G2(A), and check dim⁡Gλ=aA(λ).
  3. Verify that Q4=G1(A)⊕G2(A), and find mA.

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-c1.title: C1: The Fitting decomposition
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-c1.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n, and let N∈L(V) be any operator. Put U=kerNn and W=imNn.

  1. Prove that U∩W={0}, and deduce V=U⊕W.
  2. Prove that U and W are N-invariant, that N|U is nilpotent, and that N|W is invertible.
  3. Identify U as a generalized eigenspace of N.
  4. Compute U and W for N=(0101)∈M2(Q).

Hint: for (a), if v=Nnw and Nnv=0, look at which kernel w lies in.

exr-generalized-eigenspaces-c2.title: C2: Commuting operators preserve generalized eigenspaces
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-c2.title_html: C2: Commuting operators preserve generalized eigenspaces
exr-generalized-eigenspaces-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional, and let S,T∈L(V) with ST=TS.

  1. Prove that S(Gλ(T))⊆Gλ(T) for every λ∈F.
  2. Deduce that if pT splits, then every generalized eigenspace of T is invariant under every polynomial in T and under S, and that V has a basis in which both S and T have block diagonal matrices with blocks of sizes aT(λ1),…,aT(λk).
  3. Show by example that part (a) can be vacuous: find commuting S,T on Q2 and a λ with Eλ(T) a line, Gλ(T)=Q2, and S not a scalar multiple of the identity.

exr-jordan-canonical-form-a1.title: A1
exr-jordan-canonical-form-a1.html:
1. Define a Jordan block and a Jordan matrix, and state what a Jordan form of T is.
  2. State the Jordan Canonical Form Theorem, including the uniqueness clause.
  3. How do you read a(λ), g(λ) and the exponent of x−λ in mT off a Jordan form?
  4. True or false: every matrix in Mn(R) has a Jordan form over R. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if A and B have the same characteristic and the same minimal polynomial, they are similar. Justify your answer.
  6. Is (5104) a Jordan matrix? What is its Jordan form?

exr-jordan-canonical-form-b1.title: B1: Jordan forms from polynomial data
exr-jordan-canonical-form-b1.title_html: B1: Jordan forms from polynomial data
exr-jordan-canonical-form-b1.html:
In each case T is an operator on a complex vector space with the given characteristic and minimal polynomials. List all possible Jordan forms, up to the order of the blocks, and say what extra data would pin the answer down.

  1. pT=(x−2)4, mT=(x−2)2.
  2. pT=(x−1)3(x+1)2, mT=(x−1)3(x+1).
  3. pT=(x−5)5, mT=(x−5)3.

exr-jordan-canonical-form-b2.title: B2: Jordan forms and Jordan bases
exr-jordan-canonical-form-b2.title_html: B2: Jordan forms and Jordan bases
exr-jordan-canonical-form-b2.html:
For each matrix, find the Jordan form J and an invertible P with P−1AP=J. Verify your P by checking AP=PJ column by column.

  1. A1=(−1−1−2121102)∈M3(Q), with pA1=(x−1)3.
  2. A2=(2−1−1−34−13−23)∈M3(Q), with pA2=(x−2)2(x−5).
  3. A3=(211−2−31−1−1−3−11−1−3−1−11)∈M4(Q), with pA3=(x−2)3(x+1).

exr-jordan-canonical-form-b3.title: B3: Similar or not?
exr-jordan-canonical-form-b3.html:
Determine whether each pair of matrices is similar. Justify your answer.

  1. J2(4)⊕J1(4) and J1(4)⊕J2(4).
  2. J3(0)⊕J1(0) and J2(0)⊕J2(0).
  3. J2(1)⊕J2(1) and J2(1)⊕J1(1)⊕J1(1).
  4. diag(2,2,5) and the matrix A2 of @exr-jordan-canonical-form-b2 (b).

exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1.title: C1: A matrix is similar to its transpose
exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1.title_html: C1: A matrix is similar to its transpose
exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with pA split over F.

  1. Let R∈Mk(F) be the reversal permutation matrix, with 1 in each position (j,k+1−j) and 0 elsewhere. Prove that R−1=R and R−1Jk(λ)R=Jk(λ)T.
  2. Deduce that every Jordan matrix J satisfies J∼JT.
  3. Deduce that A∼AT.

Hint: for (c), transpose a similarity A=PJP−1. The conclusion holds over every field; Section 7 removes the hypothesis that pA splits.

exr-jordan-canonical-form-c2.title: C2: How much do p and m decide?
exr-jordan-canonical-form-c2.title_html: C2: How much do p and m decide?
exr-jordan-canonical-form-c2.html:
Work over C.

  1. Find all Jordan forms with pT=(x−1)3(x−2)2 and mT=(x−1)2(x−2).
  2. Find all Jordan forms with pT=(x−1)4(x−2)2 and mT=(x−1)2(x−2).
  3. In (b), what is the least amount of extra information that determines the Jordan form?
  4. Prove that pT and mT determine the Jordan form whenever a(λ)≤3 for every eigenvalue λ.

exr-jordan-chevalley-a1.title: A1
exr-jordan-chevalley-a1.html:
1. Define a semisimple operator, and say how the definition specializes to Chapter 8’s criterion for diagonalizability.
  2. State the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition Theorem, including all three conditions on S and N and the uniqueness clause.
  3. True or false: (0−110)∈M2(R) is semisimple. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A=D+E with D the diagonal part of A and E the off-diagonal part, then D is the semisimple part of A. Justify your answer.
  5. Which hypothesis of the uniqueness clause does the pair (D,E) of part (d) typically violate?
  6. Why does every operator commuting with T commute with the semisimple part of T?

exr-jordan-chevalley-b1.title: B1: Semisimple and nilpotent parts
exr-jordan-chevalley-b1.html:
For each matrix over Q, find the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition A=S+N and express S as a polynomial in A.

  1. A1=(3103).
  2. A2=(1203).
  3. A3=(213020005).

exr-jordan-chevalley-b2.title: B2: When is the nilpotent part zero?
exr-jordan-chevalley-b2.title_html: B2: When is the nilpotent part zero?
exr-jordan-chevalley-b2.html: Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V≥1 and let T∈L(V) with pT split, with Jordan–Chevalley decomposition T=S+N. Prove that N=0 if and only if T is diagonalizable, and that S=0 if and only if T is nilpotent.

exr-jordan-chevalley-b3.title: B3: Block diagonal matrices
exr-jordan-chevalley-b3.html: Let A1∈Mp(F) and A2∈Mq(F) have split characteristic polynomials, with Jordan–Chevalley decompositions Ai=Si+Ni. Prove that the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of A1⊕A2 is A1⊕A2=(S1⊕S2)+(N1⊕N2).

exr-jordan-chevalley-c1.title: C1: The multiplicative version
exr-jordan-chevalley-c1.html:
Call U∈L(V) unipotent if U−idV is nilpotent. Let T∈L(V) be invertible with pT split, and let T=S+N be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition.

  1. Prove that S is invertible.
  2. Prove that S−1 commutes with N, and that S−1N is nilpotent.
  3. Deduce that T=SU with S diagonalizable, U unipotent and SU=US.
  4. Prove that this multiplicative decomposition is unique: if T=S′U′ with S′ diagonalizable, U′ unipotent and S′U′=U′S′, then S′=S and U′=U.

Hint: for (d), turn the multiplicative statement into an additive one by writing T=S′+S′(U′−idV).

exr-jordan-chevalley-c2.title: C2: The parts inherit every symmetry
exr-jordan-chevalley-c2.title_html: C2: The parts inherit every symmetry
exr-jordan-chevalley-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V≥1, let T∈L(V) with pT split, and let T=S+N be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition.

  1. Prove that if X∈L(V) satisfies XT=TX, then XS=SX and XN=NX.
  2. Deduce that every T-invariant subspace is S-invariant and N-invariant, and that S and N map each Gλ(T) into itself.
  3. Give an example of a diagonalizable S and a nilpotent N with SN≠NS for which S+N is not the operator whose semisimple part is S. (So the commuting hypothesis cannot be dropped from the uniqueness statement.)

exr-nilpotent-operators-a1.title: A1
exr-nilpotent-operators-a1.html:
1. Define a nilpotent operator and its index of nilpotency.
  2. State the structure theorem for nilpotent operators, and say what a Jordan basis is.
  3. Write down the formula for the number of chains of length at least j in terms of the ranks of the powers.
  4. True or false: a singular matrix is nilpotent. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: two nilpotent matrices in Mn(F) with the same rank are similar. Justify your answer.
  6. How many similarity classes of nilpotent matrices are there in M3(F), and what are their indices of nilpotency?

exr-nilpotent-operators-b1.title: B1: Block sizes from rank data
exr-nilpotent-operators-b1.title_html: B1: Block sizes from rank data
exr-nilpotent-operators-b1.html:
In each case N is nilpotent on a space of dimension n over F. Determine the chain lengths, or explain why no such operator exists.

  1. n=7, rankN=4, rankN2=2, rankN3=1, rankN4=0.
  2. n=6, rankN=3, rankN2=1, rankN3=0.
  3. n=6, rankN=4, rankN2=3, rankN3=0.

exr-nilpotent-operators-b2.title: B2: The five classes in dimension four
exr-nilpotent-operators-b2.title_html: B2: The five classes in dimension four
exr-nilpotent-operators-b2.html:
Let F be any field.

  1. List the five partitions of 4, and for each write down the corresponding nilpotent matrix in M4(F) as a direct sum of blocks Jk(0).
  2. For each, compute rankN, rankN2, rankN3 and the index of nilpotency.
  3. Which pairs among them share the same rank? Which invariant separates each such pair?
  4. Deduce that rankN alone is not a complete invariant of nilpotent matrices, but the full list of ranks of powers is.

exr-nilpotent-operators-b3.title: B3: A Jordan basis by hand
exr-nilpotent-operators-b3.title_html: B3: A Jordan basis by hand
exr-nilpotent-operators-b3.html:
Let M=(−1−11−112−2112−2111−11)∈M4(Q).

  1. Show that M2=0 and compute rankM.
  2. Determine the chain lengths of M.
  3. Find a Jordan basis and an invertible P with P−1MP a direct sum of blocks Jk(0). Verify your answer by checking MP=PJ column by column.

Hint: for (c), the tops of the chains may be taken among the standard basis vectors.

exr-nilpotent-operators-c1.title: C1: A nilpotent matrix is similar to its transpose
exr-nilpotent-operators-c1.title_html: C1: A nilpotent matrix is similar to its transpose
exr-nilpotent-operators-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be nilpotent.

  1. Prove that AT is nilpotent and that rank(AT)j=rankAj for every j≥1.
  2. Deduce that A∼AT.
  3. For A=J3(0), find an explicit P with P−1AP=AT.

exr-nilpotent-operators-c2.title: C2: One long chain
exr-nilpotent-operators-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let N∈L(V) be nilpotent with Nn−1≠0.

  1. Prove that there is a basis of V in which the matrix of N is Jn(0).
  2. Deduce that mN=pN=xn, and that nullityN=1.
  3. Show that the conclusion of (a) fails for N=J2(0)⊕J1(0) on a space of dimension 3, and say which hypothesis fails.

Hint: for (a), take a vector outside kerNn−1, which exists precisely because Nn−1≠0.

exr-rational-canonical-form-a1.title: A1
exr-rational-canonical-form-a1.html:
1. State the Cyclic Decomposition Theorem, including the divisibility chain and what dr and ∏jdj are.
  2. Define the invariant factors and the elementary divisors of T.
  3. What is the rational canonical form of T, and over which fields does it exist?
  4. True or false: two matrices in Mn(Q) that are similar over C are similar over Q. Justify your answer.
  5. An operator on a 5-dimensional Q-space has pT=(x−3)5 and mT=(x−3)2. What are its elementary divisors and invariant factors?
  6. True or false: r=1 if and only if T is cyclic. Justify your answer.

exr-rational-canonical-form-b1.title: B1: Invariant factors from given data
exr-rational-canonical-form-b1.title_html: B1: Invariant factors from given data
exr-rational-canonical-form-b1.html:
In each case T is an operator on a Q-vector space with the stated characteristic and minimal polynomials. Find the elementary divisors, the invariant factors, and the rational canonical form (@thm-rational-canonical-form).

  1. pT=(x−2)4, mT=(x−2)2.
  2. pT=(x2−2)3, mT=(x2−2)2.
  3. pT=(x−1)2(x+1)2, mT=(x−1)(x+1).

exr-rational-canonical-form-b2.title: B2: Rational forms of matrices
exr-rational-canonical-form-b2.html:
For each matrix, find pA, mA, the invariant factors, the rational canonical form (@thm-rational-canonical-form) and the elementary divisor form (@thm-elementary-divisor-form).

  1. A1=(010001100)∈M3(Q).
  2. A2=diag(1,1,2)∈M3(Q).
  3. A3=(0−1001000000−10010)∈M4(Q).

exr-rational-canonical-form-b3.title: B3: Counting similarity classes over a finite field
exr-rational-canonical-form-b3.title_html: B3: Counting similarity classes over a finite field
exr-rational-canonical-form-b3.html:
Work over F=F2. For each polynomial p, find the number of similarity classes of matrices A∈M3(F2) with pA=p, and list the invariant factors of each class.

  1. p=(x+1)3.
  2. p=x(x+1)2.
  3. p=x3+x+1.

Hint: by @cor-similar-iff-same-invariant-factors, a class is a way of writing p=d1⋯dr with d1∣⋯∣dr.

exr-rational-canonical-form-c1.title: C1: Which matrices are companion matrices
exr-rational-canonical-form-c1.title_html: C1: Which matrices are companion matrices
exr-rational-canonical-form-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with n≥1.

  1. Prove that A is similar to a companion matrix if and only if mA=pA, and that the companion matrix is then C(pA).
  2. Deduce that A is similar to a companion matrix if and only if its rational canonical form has exactly one block.
  3. Give an example of a matrix in M2(F) that is not similar to any companion matrix.

exr-rational-canonical-form-c2.title: C2: All similarity classes of two by two matrices over the smallest field
exr-rational-canonical-form-c2.title_html:
C2: All similarity classes of two by two matrices over the smallest
field
exr-rational-canonical-form-c2.html:
Work over F=F2, so that M2(F2) has 16 elements.

  1. List the four monic polynomials of degree 2 over F2 and factor each into irreducibles.
  2. For each, list the possible lists of invariant factors of a matrix A∈M2(F2) with that characteristic polynomial.
  3. Conclude the total number of similarity classes in M2(F2), and give a representative of each.
  4. Check your count against the orbit sizes: |GL2(F2)|=6, and the class of A has 6/|{P:P−1AP=A}| elements.

exr-rational-canonical-form-c3.title: C3: A matrix over the rationals is similar to its transpose
exr-rational-canonical-form-c3.title_html: C3: A matrix over the rationals is similar to its transpose
exr-rational-canonical-form-c3.html:
1. Let A,B∈Mn(Q) have the same Jordan form over C. Prove that A and B are similar over Q.
  2. Deduce that A∼AT over Q for every A∈Mn(Q).
  3. Which step of (b) would fail for a general field K in place of Q?

Hint for (b): @exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1.

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-a1.title: A1
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-a1.html:
1. Write down Λ(λ) for λ=a+bi and C2(λ), and say what their sizes are.
  2. State the Real Jordan Form Theorem.
  3. True or false: every matrix in Mn(R) is similar over R to an upper triangular real matrix. Justify your answer.
  4. Let A∈M6(R) have complex eigenvalues 2,2,1+i,1−i,1+i,1−i. What are the possible real Jordan forms?
  5. Define the Weyr structure of an eigenvalue and say how it is computed from T.
  6. What is the Weyr form of J3(7)? And of 7I3?

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b1.title: B1: Real forms of two by two matrices
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b1.title_html: B1: Real forms of two by two matrices
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b1.html:
For each real matrix, find the complex eigenvalues, the real Jordan form (@thm-real-jordan-form), and an invertible P∈M2(R) putting it in that form. Verify AP=PΛ column by column.

  1. A1=(12−21).
  2. A2=(3−51−1).

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b2.title: B2: Weyr forms of Jordan matrices
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b2.title_html: B2: Weyr forms of Jordan matrices
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b2.html:
For each Jordan matrix, write down the block sizes, the Weyr structure of each eigenvalue, and the Weyr form (@thm-weyr-form).

  1. J3(0)⊕J2(0)⊕J1(0)∈M6(F).
  2. J2(4)⊕J1(4)⊕J1(9)∈M4(F).
  3. J2(0)⊕J2(0)∈M4(F).

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b3.title: B3: Real forms of three by three matrices from the characteristic polynomial
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b3.title_html:
B3: Real forms of three by three matrices from the characteristic
polynomial
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-b3.html:
For each characteristic polynomial, list all possible real Jordan forms (@thm-real-jordan-form) of a matrix A∈M3(R) with that polynomial.

  1. pA=(x−2)(x2+1).
  2. pA=(x+1)(x2−2x+5).
  3. pA=(x−1)3.
  4. pA=(x2+1)(x−1) but with A required to be diagonalizable over R. Is this possible?

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c1.title: C1: The real form of a companion matrix
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c1.title_html: C1: The real form of a companion matrix
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c1.html:
Let p=(x2+1)2=x4+2x2+1∈R[x] and let C=C(p)∈M4(R) be its companion matrix, with 1 in each position just below the diagonal and last column (−1,0,−2,0) (@exr-characteristic-polynomial-c1).

  1. Write down C, and explain why pC=mC=p.
  2. Determine the complex Jordan form of C.
  3. Deduce the real Jordan form of C.
  4. Verify your answer by comparing traces and characteristic polynomials.

Hint: for (b), the exponent of x−i in mC is the largest size of an i-block.

exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c2.title: C2: Commuting with a Weyr matrix, and with a Jordan matrix
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c2.title_html: C2: Commuting with a Weyr matrix, and with a Jordan matrix
exr-real-jordan-and-weyr-forms-c2.html:
Let F be a field.

  1. Let W∈M3(F) be the basic Weyr matrix with λ=0 and structure (2,1) (@def-weyr-form). Find all K∈M3(F) with WK=KW, and check that they are block upper triangular for the partition 3=2+1.
  2. Let J=J2(0)⊕J1(0). Find all K∈M3(F) with JK=KJ, and exhibit one that is not upper triangular. Which partition of 3 does it violate?
  3. Compute the dimension of each of the two commutants, and explain why they are equal.

exr-smith-normal-form-a1.title: A1
exr-smith-normal-form-a1.html:
1. List the three elementary operations over F[x], and say which one differs from its counterpart over a field and why.
  2. State a criterion for a matrix U∈Mn(F[x]) to be invertible in Mn(F[x]).
  3. State the Smith Normal Form theorem, including the uniqueness clause.
  4. Define the k-th determinantal divisor of a polynomial matrix, and say why it is unchanged by equivalence.
  5. True or false: if det(xI−A)=det(xI−B), then xI−A≈xI−B. Justify your answer.
  6. How do you read mA off the Smith normal form of xI−A?

exr-smith-normal-form-b1.title: B1: Smith normal forms
exr-smith-normal-form-b1.html:
Find the Smith normal form over Q[x] of each of the following, naming the operations you use.

  1. M1=(xx+1x−1x).
  2. M2=(x2−100x2−x).
  3. M3=(x01−1x00−1x).

exr-smith-normal-form-b2.title: B2: Invariant factors from determinantal divisors
exr-smith-normal-form-b2.title_html: B2: Invariant factors from determinantal divisors
exr-smith-normal-form-b2.html:
For each matrix A, compute Δ1,…,Δn of xI−A, write down the Smith normal form, and read off the invariant factors, mA and the Jordan form.

  1. A=J2(0)⊕J2(0)∈M4(Q).
  2. A=J3(0)⊕J1(0)∈M4(Q).
  3. A=(3103)∈M2(Q).

exr-smith-normal-form-b3.title: B3: Deciding similarity
exr-smith-normal-form-b3.html:
Determine whether each pair is similar over the stated field. Justify your answer using @thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent.

  1. A=(0−110) and B=(01−10) over Q.
  2. A=(21−212−211−1) and B=J2(1)⊕J1(1) over Q.
  3. A=(0−210) and B=(0−120) over Q.

exr-smith-normal-form-c1.title: C1: The same algorithm over the integers
exr-smith-normal-form-c1.title_html: C1: The same algorithm over the integers
exr-smith-normal-form-c1.html:
The proof of @thm-smith-normal-form used only one property of F[x]: division with remainder, where the “size” of a non-zero element is its degree. The integers Z have the same property, with |a| in place of deg.

  1. State the version of @thm-smith-normal-form for M∈Mn(Z) that the same proof gives, saying what replaces “monic”.
  2. Compute the Smith normal form over Z of M=(2464), naming the operations.
  3. Every finite abelian group G with n generators is Zn modulo the column span of some M∈Mn(Z), the matrix of relations, exactly as V was F[x]n modulo the columns of xI−A. Using (b), identify the group with relation matrix M as a product of cyclic groups.

Hint: for (c), a diagonal relation matrix diag(d1,…,dn) presents the product of the cyclic groups Z/diZ.

exr-smith-normal-form-c2.title: C2: Uniqueness by hand in the smallest case
exr-smith-normal-form-c2.title_html: C2: Uniqueness by hand in the smallest case
exr-smith-normal-form-c2.html:
Let M∈M2(F[x]) be non-zero.

  1. Prove directly, without using determinantal divisors, that Δ1(M) — the monic gcd of the four entries of M — is unchanged by each of the six elementary operations of @def-polynomial-elementary-operations.
  2. Prove that det(UMV)=cdetM for a non-zero constant c whenever U,V are invertible over F[x].
  3. Deduce that if diag(d1,d2)≈diag(e1,e2) with all four entries monic or zero, d1∣d2 and e1∣e2, then d1=e1 and d2=e2.

lem-annihilator-of-sum.title: Annihilator of a Sum with Coprime Annihilators
lem-annihilator-of-sum.title_html: Annihilator of a Sum with Coprime Annihilators
lem-annihilator-of-sum.html: Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and u,w∈V with f=mT,u and g=mT,w coprime. Then mT,u+w=fg. More generally, if v1,…,vk∈V have pairwise coprime T-annihilators f1,…,fk, then mT,v1+⋯+vk=f1f2⋯fk.

lem-jordan-chain-independent.title: A Jordan Chain Is Independent
lem-jordan-chain-independent.html:
Let N∈L(V) and let (Nk−1u,…,Nu,u) be a Jordan chain, so Nku=0≠Nk−1u. Then:

  1. the list is linearly independent, so k≤dim⁡V when V is finite-dimensional;
  2. C=span(u,Nu,…,Nk−1u) is N-invariant of dimension k, and the matrix of N|C in the chain, taken in the order of @def-jordan-chain, is Jk(0).

lem-matrix-polynomial-division.title: Division of a Polynomial Matrix by xI - A
lem-matrix-polynomial-division.title_html: Division of a Polynomial Matrix by xI−A
lem-matrix-polynomial-division.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and M∈Mn(F[x]). Then there are Q∈Mn(F[x]) and R∈Mn(F) with M=(xI−A)Q+R.

lem-minimal-polynomial-field-extension.title: The Minimal Polynomial Does Not Notice a Larger Field
lem-minimal-polynomial-field-extension.title_html: The Minimal Polynomial Does Not Notice a Larger Field
lem-minimal-polynomial-field-extension.html: Let K⊆L be fields and A∈Mn(K), n≥1. Then the minimal polynomial of A computed in K[x] equals the minimal polynomial of A computed in L[x].

lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block.title: A Polynomial of a Jordan Block
lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block.title_html: A Polynomial of a Jordan Block
lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block.html: Let F have characteristic 0, let k≥1, λ∈F and p∈F[x]. Then p(Jk(λ)) is the upper triangular matrix whose (r,r+j)-entry is (p(Jk(λ)))r,r+j=p(j)(λ)j!(0≤j≤k−1, 1≤r≤k−j), with all entries below the diagonal equal to 0. In particular the value p(λ) fills the diagonal, p′(λ) the superdiagonal, and only the first k derivatives of p at λ are involved.

lem-powers-transfer-along-similarity.title: Convergence and Boundedness Survive a Similarity
lem-powers-transfer-along-similarity.title_html: Convergence and Boundedness Survive a Similarity
lem-powers-transfer-along-similarity.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(C) with B=P−1AP for an invertible P∈Mn(C), and let L∈Mn(C). Then:

  1. Am→L if and only if Bm→P−1LP;
  2. (Am) is bounded if and only if (Bm) is bounded.

lem-rank-field-independent.title: Rank Does Not Change with the Field
lem-rank-field-independent.title_html: Rank Does Not Change with the Field
lem-rank-field-independent.html: Let K be a subfield of a field L and let M∈Mm×n(K). Then the rank of M computed over K equals its rank computed over L.

lem-real-null-space-complexifies.title: Real and Complex Null Spaces of a Real Matrix
lem-real-null-space-complexifies.title_html: Real and Complex Null Spaces of a Real Matrix
lem-real-null-space-complexifies.html:
Let M∈Mn(R), let U={x∈Rn:Mx=0} be its null space over R, and let U~={z∈Cn:Mz=0} be its null space over C. Then:

  1. for z=x+iy with x,y∈Rn: z∈U~ if and only if x∈U and y∈U;
  2. every basis of U over R is a basis of U~ over C; in particular dimR⁡U=dimC⁡U~ and rankM is the same computed over R and over C.

lem-realify-jordan-chain.title: Realifying a Conjugate Pair of Chains
lem-realify-jordan-chain.title_html: Realifying a Conjugate Pair of Chains
lem-realify-jordan-chain.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), let λ=a+bi with a,b∈R and b≠0, and let (w1,…,wk) be a Jordan chain of A for λ in Cn, so that (A−λI)w1=0and(A−λI)wj=wj−1(2≤j≤k). Write wj=uj−ivj with uj,vj∈Rn, and put u0=v0=0. Then:

  1. Auj=auj+bvj+uj−1 and Avj=−buj+avj+vj−1 for 1≤j≤k;
  2. (w1―,…,wk―) is a Jordan chain of A for λ―;
  3. the 2k vectors u1,v1,…,uk,vk span, over C, the same subspace of Cn as the 2k vectors w1,…,wk,w1―,…,wk―, and one of the two lists is linearly independent over C if and only if the other is;
  4. if the 2k vectors u1,v1,…,uk,vk are linearly independent over R, then U=span(u1,v1,…,uk,vk)⊆Rn is invariant under A, and the matrix of TA|U in the ordered basis (u1,v1,…,uk,vk) is Ck(λ).

prp-cyclic-subspace-smallest.title: The Cyclic Subspace Is the Smallest Invariant Subspace Containing the Vector
prp-cyclic-subspace-smallest.title_html:
The Cyclic Subspace Is the Smallest Invariant Subspace Containing the
Vector
prp-cyclic-subspace-smallest.html:
Let V be a vector space over F, T∈L(V) and v∈V. Then:

  1. Z(v;T)={p(T)v:p∈F[x]};
  2. Z(v;T) is T-invariant;
  3. if U is a T-invariant subspace of V with v∈U, then Z(v;T)⊆U.

prp-elementary-divisors-from-kernels.title: Counting the Exponents
prp-elementary-divisors-from-kernels.html:
Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F, let T∈L(V), and suppose V=Z(u1;T)⊕⋯⊕Z(uN;T),mT,ui=gi, with every gi monic and non-constant. Then for every monic irreducible p∈F[x]:

  1. dim⁡kerp(T)k=deg⁡p⋅∑i=1Nmin(k,vp(gi)) for every integer k≥0;
  2. for every k≥1, #{i:vp(gi)≥k}=dim⁡kerp(T)k−dim⁡kerp(T)k−1deg⁡p, a number depending only on T, p and k.

prp-nilpotent-basic.title: Basic Properties of Nilpotent Operators
prp-nilpotent-basic.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let N∈L(V). Then:

  1. N is nilpotent if and only if Nn=0, if and only if G0(N)=V;
  2. if N is nilpotent with index s, then s≤n, mN=xs and pN=xn;
  3. if N is nilpotent, then spec(N)={0}, and there is a basis in which the matrix of N is upper triangular with zero diagonal;
  4. conversely, if pN=xn, then N is nilpotent.

prp-operations-are-equivalence.title: Operations and Equivalence
prp-operations-are-equivalence.html:
Let M,M′∈Mn(F[x]).

  1. ≈ is an equivalence relation on Mn(F[x]).
  2. If M′ is obtained from M by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations over F[x], then M≈M′.

prp-polynomial-matrix-invertible.title: Invertible Polynomial Matrices
prp-polynomial-matrix-invertible.html: Let U∈Mn(F[x]). Then U has an inverse in Mn(F[x]) if and only if detU is a non-zero constant.

prp-semisimple-iff-diagonalizable-over-e.title: Semisimple Means Diagonalizable After Enlarging the Field
prp-semisimple-iff-diagonalizable-over-e.title_html: Semisimple Means Diagonalizable After Enlarging the Field
prp-semisimple-iff-diagonalizable-over-e.html: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let A∈Mn(K) with n≥1, and let L⊇K be a field over which mA splits. Then A is semisimple over K⟺A is diagonalizable over L.

prp-vector-with-full-annihilator.title: Some Vector Has the Minimal Polynomial as Its Annihilator
prp-vector-with-full-annihilator.title_html: Some Vector Has the Minimal Polynomial as Its Annihilator
prp-vector-with-full-annihilator.html: Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and T∈L(V). Then there is v∈V with mT,v=mT.

prp-weyr-commutant.title: The Commutant of a Basic Weyr Matrix Is Block Triangular
prp-weyr-commutant.title_html: The Commutant of a Basic Weyr Matrix Is Block Triangular
prp-weyr-commutant.html: Let W∈Mm(F) be a basic Weyr matrix with eigenvalue λ and Weyr structure (w1,…,ws), and let K∈Mm(F) satisfy WK=KW. Then K is block upper triangular for the partition m=w1+⋯+ws: its blocks Kpq vanish for p>q.

thm-companion-char-min.title: The Companion Matrix Realizes Its Polynomial Twice
thm-companion-char-min.title_html: The Companion Matrix Realizes Its Polynomial Twice
thm-companion-char-min.html: Let p∈F[x] be monic of degree n≥1 and C=C(p). Then pC=mC=p, and e1 satisfies Z(e1;C)=Fn with mC,e1=p. Consequently every monic polynomial over F is both the characteristic and the minimal polynomial of some square matrix over F.

thm-cyclic-decomposition.title: Cyclic Decomposition Theorem
thm-cyclic-decomposition.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and let T∈L(V). Then there are an integer r≥1, vectors v1,…,vr∈V and monic non-constant polynomials d1,…,dr∈F[x] such that V=Z(v1;T)⊕⋯⊕Z(vr;T),mT,vj=dj, and

  1. d1∣d2∣⋯∣dr;
  2. dr=mT;
  3. d1d2⋯dr=pT; in particular ∑jdeg⁡dj=dim⁡V;
  4. there is a finer decomposition V=⨁i,jZ(vij;T) into cyclic subspaces whose annihilators mT,vij are powers of monic irreducibles, and the list of these prime powers, with repetitions, consists exactly of the prime powers occurring in the factorizations of d1,…,dr.

thm-cyclic-iff-min-equals-char.title: Cyclic Operators
thm-cyclic-iff-min-equals-char.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent:

  1. T is cyclic, that is, T has a cyclic vector;
  2. deg⁡mT=n;
  3. mT=pT.

In that case v is a cyclic vector if and only if mT,v=mT, and in the basis (v,Tv,…,Tn−1v) the matrix of T is C(mT). The same holds for A∈Mn(F).

thm-cyclic-subspace-basis.title: Basis and Matrix of a Cyclic Subspace
thm-cyclic-subspace-basis.title_html: Basis and Matrix of a Cyclic Subspace
thm-cyclic-subspace-basis.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V) and let v∈V with v≠0. Write Z=Z(v;T) and mT,v=xk+ak−1xk−1+⋯+a1x+a0,k=deg⁡mT,v≥1. Then:

  1. (v, Tv, …, Tk−1v) is a basis of Z; in particular dim⁡Z=deg⁡mT,v;
  2. Tkv=−(a0v+a1Tv+⋯+ak−1Tk−1v), and the matrix of T|Z in the basis of (a) is the companion matrix of mT,v (@exr-characteristic-polynomial-c1; the definition is repeated in full as @def-companion-matrix below);
  3. mT|Z=pT|Z=mT,v;
  4. mT,v∣mT, and deg⁡mT,v≤deg⁡mT≤dim⁡V.

thm-elementary-divisor-form.title: Elementary Divisor Form
thm-elementary-divisor-form.html: Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F, let T∈L(V), and let q1,…,qN be the elementary divisors of T. Then there is a basis B of V with [T]B=C(q1)⊕C(q2)⊕⋯⊕C(qN), and the blocks are determined by T up to their order.

thm-exponential-properties.title: Properties of the Matrix Exponential
thm-exponential-properties.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(C) and let P∈Mn(C) be invertible.

  1. e0=I and eP−1AP=P−1eAP.
  2. The function R→Mn(C), t↦etA, is differentiable entrywise, with ddtetA=AetA=etAA.
  3. eA is invertible, with (eA)−1=e−A.
  4. If AB=BA, then eA+B=eAeB.
  5. deteA=etrA.

thm-exponential-series-converges.title: The Exponential Series Converges to the Jordan Definition
thm-exponential-series-converges.title_html: The Exponential Series Converges to the Jordan Definition
thm-exponential-series-converges.html: Let A∈Mn(C). Then the series ∑mAm/m! converges entrywise, and its sum is the matrix exp⁡(A) given by @def-matrix-function-jordan for the function f=exp. In particular, for a single Jordan block, eJk(λ)=eλ(1112!⋯1(k−1)!11⋱⋮⋱⋱12!111), the upper triangular matrix with eλ/j! in every position (r,r+j).

thm-generalized-eigenspace-decomposition.title: Generalized Eigenspace Decomposition
thm-generalized-eigenspace-decomposition.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, let T∈L(V), and suppose pT splits over F, with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk and pT=(x−λ1)a1⋯(x−λk)ak,mT=(x−λ1)s1⋯(x−λk)sk, where ai=aT(λi) and 1≤si≤ai. Write Gi=Gλi(T) and Ni=(T−λiidV)|Gi. Then:

  1. Gi=ker(T−λiidV)si, and V=G1⊕G2⊕⋯⊕Gk;
  2. each Gi is T-invariant and non-zero, with Eλi(T)⊆Gi, and Eλi(T)=Gi if and only if si=1;
  3. dim⁡Gi=ai and pT|Gi=(x−λi)ai;
  4. Niai=0; that is, T|Gi=λiidGi+Ni with Ni nilpotent, of stabilization index si;
  5. if B is a basis of V obtained by writing bases of G1,…,Gk one after another, then [T]B=[T|G1] ⊕ … ⊕ [T|Gk] is block diagonal, with the i-th block of size ai.

thm-jordan-canonical-form.title: Jordan Canonical Form Theorem
thm-jordan-canonical-form.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V).

  1. (Existence) T has a Jordan form if and only if pT splits over F.
  2. (Uniqueness) Suppose J is a Jordan form of T. Then for every λ∈F and every integer j≥1, the number of blocks Jk(λ) in J with k≥j equals rank(T−λidV)j−1−rank(T−λidV)j, a number depending only on T, λ and j. Consequently any two Jordan forms of T have the same blocks, up to the order in which they are listed.

Equivalently, for A∈Mn(F) with pA split: A is similar to a Jordan matrix, and that matrix is unique up to the order of its blocks. We call it the Jordan form of A.

thm-jordan-chevalley.title: Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
thm-jordan-chevalley.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V) with pT split over F. Then:

  1. (Existence) There are S,N∈L(V) with T=S+N,S diagonalizable,N nilpotent,SN=NS; moreover S=g(T) and N=h(T) for some g,h∈F[x].
  2. (Uniqueness) If T=S′+N′ with S′ diagonalizable, N′ nilpotent and S′N′=N′S′, then S′=S and N′=N.

We call S the semisimple part and N the nilpotent part of T.

thm-kernel-chain-stabilizes.title: The Kernel Chain Stabilizes
thm-kernel-chain-stabilizes.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n, let N∈L(V), and write Kk=kerNk for k≥0, so that K0={0}. Then:

  1. K0⊆K1⊆K2⊆…, and every Kk is N-invariant;
  2. if Km=Km+1 for some m≥0, then Km+j=Km for every j≥0;
  3. there is a least index s≥0 with Ks=Ks+1; it satisfies s≤n, the inclusions K0⊊K1⊊⋯⊊Ks are strict, and Kk=Ks for every k≥s;
  4. in particular kerNn=kerNn+j for every j≥0.

thm-linear-ode-solution.title: Solution of a Linear System
thm-linear-ode-solution.html: Let A∈Mn(C) and x0∈Cn. Then the function x(t)=etAx0(t∈R) is differentiable and satisfies x′(t)=Ax(t) for all t and x(0)=x0; and it is the only differentiable function R→Cn with these two properties.

thm-matrix-function-hermite.title: Functions of a Matrix Are Polynomials in It
thm-matrix-function-hermite.title_html: Functions of a Matrix Are Polynomials in It
thm-matrix-function-hermite.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) with distinct eigenvalues μ1,…,μd, and write mA=(x−μ1)s1⋯(x−μd)sd, so that sl is the largest size of a μl-block of the Jordan form of A (@cor-jordan-invariants (c)). Let f be as in @def-matrix-function-jordan. Then:

  1. there is a polynomial p∈C[x] with deg⁡p<deg⁡mA and p(j)(μl)=f(j)(μl)for all l=1,…,d and j=0,…,sl−1, and p is the only such polynomial of degree less than deg⁡mA;
  2. for every polynomial q∈C[x] satisfying those deg⁡mA equations, q(A)=p(A);
  3. f(A)=p(A). In particular f(A) does not depend on the choice of P or on the order of the blocks, and f(A) is determined by the finitely many numbers f(j)(μl).

The polynomial p of (a) is the Hermite interpolating polynomial of f on the spectrum of A.

thm-matrix-powers-bounded.title: Power-Bounded Matrices
thm-matrix-powers-bounded.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, with Jordan form J. The sequence (Am)m≥0 is bounded if and only if

  1. every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies |λ|≤1, and
  2. every eigenvalue λ with |λ|=1 has all of its blocks in J of size 1, equivalently aA(λ)=gA(λ), equivalently x−λ occurs to the first power in mA.

thm-matrix-powers-converge.title: Convergent Matrices
thm-matrix-powers-converge.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, with Jordan form J. Then (Am) converges if and only if every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies

  1. |λ|<1, or
  2. λ=1 and all of its blocks in J have size 1.

In that case limm→∞Am=Π, where Π∈Mn(C) is the matrix, in the standard basis, of the projection onto E1(A) along ⨁λ≠1Gλ(A) if 1∈spec(A), and Π=0 otherwise.

thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero.title: Powers Tending to Zero
thm-matrix-powers-converge-to-zero.html: Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1. Then Am→0 if and only if every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies |λ|<1.

thm-neumann-series-spectral.title: Neumann Series
thm-neumann-series-spectral.html: Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1. Then the series ∑k≥0Ak converges if and only if every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies |λ|<1. In that case I−A is invertible and ∑k=0∞Ak=(I−A)−1.

thm-nilpotent-block-sizes-from-ranks.title: Block Sizes from Ranks of Powers
thm-nilpotent-block-sizes-from-ranks.title_html: Block Sizes from Ranks of Powers
thm-nilpotent-block-sizes-from-ranks.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, let N∈L(V) be nilpotent, and suppose B is a Jordan basis for N with chain lengths k1≥⋯≥kr≥1, as in @thm-nilpotent-structure. Write rj=rankNj for j≥0, so r0=n. Then:

  1. for every integer j≥0, rankNj=∑i=1rmax(ki−j,0)anddim⁡kerNj=∑i=1rmin(ki,j);
  2. for every integer j≥1, the number of chains of length at least j is #{i:ki≥j}=rj−1−rj;
  3. for every integer j≥1, the number of chains of length exactly j is #{i:ki=j}=rj−1−2rj+rj+1;
  4. consequently the list k1≥⋯≥kr is determined by N alone: any two Jordan bases for N have the same chain lengths. Moreover r=n−rankN=nullityN and k1 is the index of nilpotency of N.

thm-nilpotent-structure.title: Structure Theorem for Nilpotent Operators
thm-nilpotent-structure.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let N∈L(V) be nilpotent. Then there are an integer r≥1, vectors u1,…,ur∈V and integers k1≥k2≥⋯≥kr≥1,k1+k2+⋯+kr=n, such that:

  1. Nkiui=0 for each i, and the list B obtained by writing the r Jordan chains one after another, B=(Nk1−1u1,…,Nu1,u1⏟chain 1, …, Nkr−1ur,…,Nur,ur⏟chain r), is a basis of V;
  2. with Ci=span(ui,Nui,…,Nki−1ui), each Ci is N-invariant, V=C1⊕⋯⊕Cr, and [N]B=Jk1(0)⊕Jk2(0)⊕⋯⊕Jkr(0).

thm-primary-cyclic-decomposition.title: Cyclic Decomposition for a Single Prime Power
thm-primary-cyclic-decomposition.title_html: Cyclic Decomposition for a Single Prime Power
thm-primary-cyclic-decomposition.html: Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V), and suppose mT=pe,p∈F[x] monic irreducible of degree d,e≥1. Then there are an integer m≥1, vectors u1,…,um∈V and exponents e=k1≥k2≥⋯≥km≥1 such that V=Z(u1;T)⊕Z(u2;T)⊕⋯⊕Z(um;T),mT,ui=pki(1≤i≤m). In particular dim⁡V=d(k1+⋯+km).

thm-rational-canonical-form.title: Rational Canonical Form
thm-rational-canonical-form.html: Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over any field F, and let T∈L(V) have invariant factors d1∣d2∣⋯∣dr. Then there is a basis B of V with [T]B=C(d1)⊕C(d2)⊕⋯⊕C(dr), and this matrix is determined by T. It is called the rational canonical form of T. Equivalently, every A∈Mn(F) with n≥1 is similar to exactly one matrix of the form C(d1)⊕⋯⊕C(dr) with d1∣⋯∣dr monic and non-constant.

thm-real-jordan-form.title: Real Jordan Form
thm-real-jordan-form.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with n≥1. List the eigenvalues of A in C as μ1,…,μp∈R(the real ones, distinct),λ1,λ1―,…,λq,λq―(the conjugate pairs, with Imλt>0).

  1. (Existence) There is an invertible P∈Mn(R) such that P−1AP is a real Jordan matrix (@def-real-jordan-block), in which the blocks for a real eigenvalue μl are ordinary Jordan blocks Jk(μl) and the blocks for a pair {λt,λt―} are real Jordan blocks Ck(λt).
  2. (Uniqueness) In any such matrix, the number of blocks Jk(μ) with k≥j, for μ∈R, and the number of blocks Ck(λ) with k≥j, for λ∉R, both equal rank(A−νI)j−1−rank(A−νI)j(ν=μ resp. ν=λ), the ranks being computed over C in the second case. Consequently the real Jordan matrix is determined by A up to the order of its blocks.

thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent.title: Similarity as Equivalence of xI - A and xI - B
thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent.title_html: Similarity as Equivalence of xI−A and xI−B
thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent.html: Let F be a field, n≥1 and A,B∈Mn(F). Then A∼Bover F⟺xI−A≈xI−Bover F[x].

thm-smith-normal-form.title: Smith Normal Form
thm-smith-normal-form.html:
Let F be a field, n≥1 and M∈Mn(F[x]). Then:

  1. (Existence) M is equivalent over F[x], by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations, to a diagonal matrix D=diag(d1,d2,…,dn) in which every di is monic or zero and di∣di+1 for i=1,…,n−1.
  2. (Uniqueness) The list (d1,…,dn) is determined by M: if M≈diag(d1,…,dn)≈diag(e1,…,en) with both lists as in (a), then di=ei for every i.

The matrix D is called the Smith normal form of M, and d1,…,dn its invariant divisors.

thm-weyr-form.title: Weyr Form
thm-weyr-form.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V).

  1. (Existence) T has a Weyr form if and only if pT splits over F. One can be arranged with one basic Weyr block per eigenvalue.
  2. (Uniqueness) In any Weyr form of T with one basic block per eigenvalue, the block for λ has Weyr structure wj=dim⁡ker(T−λidV)j−dim⁡ker(T−λidV)j−1(j≥1), the non-zero terms of this sequence; equivalently (w1,w2,…) is the dual partition of the partition formed by the sizes of the λ-blocks of the Jordan form of T. So the Weyr form is determined by T up to the order of its basic blocks.
